lead: Replace the BJT base with a MOSFET gate and three signal-ground choices remain. Common source (CS) grounds the source, common gate (CG) grounds the gate, and common drain (CD) grounds the drain; CD is also called a source follower. The gate draws almost no current, so the BJT input-resistance problem disappears. CS gives voltage gain and inversion, CG gives low input resistance, and CD gives gain just below one with low output resistance. These stages appear in sensor front ends, radio-frequency input stages, and output buffers inside op-amps.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.3 for the bias point and the square law, and Chapter 2.4 for the small-signal idea.

blocks.text: At the bias point the MOSFET sits in saturation. Write the square law as I<sub>D</sub> = K<sub>n</sub>(V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>TN</sub>)². Here I<sub>D</sub> is the DC drain current in A, V<sub>GS</sub> is the DC gate-source voltage in V, V<sub>TN</sub> is the threshold voltage in V, and K<sub>n</sub> is the device parameter in A/V². Some books put a factor ½ inside K<sub>n</sub>; check the definition first.

blocks.where: g<sub>m</sub> is transconductance in A/V (also called siemens, S); K<sub>n</sub> is the device parameter in A/V²; I<sub>D</sub> is the DC drain current in A; V<sub>GS</sub> is the DC gate-source voltage in V; V<sub>TN</sub> is the threshold voltage in V.

blocks.text: For small signals, let v<sub>gs</sub> be a small change in gate-source voltage and v<sub>ds</sub> a small change in drain-source voltage. The drain current gets an AC part g<sub>m</sub>v<sub>gs</sub> plus a part v<sub>ds</sub>/r<sub>o</sub>. The gate current is zero at low frequency, so the gate is an open circuit. This one fact separates MOSFET stages from BJT stages.

blocks.where: r<sub>o</sub> is the small-signal output resistance in Ω; λ is the channel-length modulation parameter in V⁻¹; I<sub>D</sub> is the DC drain current in A.

blocks.text: The model is a dependent current source g<sub>m</sub>v<sub>gs</sub> from drain to source, in parallel with r<sub>o</sub>. Bias sets g<sub>m</sub> and r<sub>o</sub>. In a long-channel device r<sub>o</sub> is large; in a short-channel device λ is larger and r<sub>o</sub> cannot be dropped.
In a CS stage the input is at the gate, the source is at AC ground, and the output is at the drain through RD to VDD. RL stands for the next stage or load. Bias from Chapter 2.3 sets ID and VDS.

blocks.where: A<sub>v</sub> is the small-signal voltage gain, unitless; g<sub>m</sub> is transconductance in S; R<sub>D</sub> is the drain bias resistor in Ω; R<sub>L</sub> is the load resistance in Ω; r<sub>o</sub> is the MOSFET output resistance in Ω.

blocks.text: The minus sign means inversion: a rising gate voltage increases drain current, so the drain voltage falls. Input resistance is very high; bias resistors set it in practice. Output resistance is R<sub>D</sub> ∥ r<sub>o</sub>.

The CS stage is the workhorse voltage amplifier: after a sensor, after a filter, inside op-amp gain stages. Its response is flat in the middle band and falls at high frequency because of MOSFET capacitances, covered in Unit 3. The figure normalizes both curves to 40 dB: a typical CS stage rolls off near 100 kHz, while a source follower holds its response to about 10 MHz.

In a CG stage the input is at the source, the gate is at AC ground, and the output is at the drain. Input resistance is low, about 1/gm. The signal current entering the source leaves the drain almost unchanged, so current gain is near one. Voltage gain is positive, about +gm(RD ∥ RL ∥ ro), so the stage does not invert. It serves as a low-noise input stage and as the input half of a cascode, see Chapter 2.8.

In a CD stage, also called a source follower, the input is at the gate, the drain is at AC ground, and the output is at the source across R<sub>s</sub>. Use R<sub>s</sub> ∥ R<sub>L</sub> when a load is present.

blocks.where: A<sub>v</sub> is the small-signal voltage gain, unitless and below 1; g<sub>m</sub> is transconductance in S; R<sub>s</sub> is the source resistance in Ω, replaced by R<sub>s</sub> ∥ R<sub>L</sub> when a load is connected.

blocks.text: The source follower does not invert, has gain just below one, and has low output resistance, about 1/g<sub>m</sub> ∥ R<sub>s</sub>. It buffers: it takes a high-resistance signal and drives a low-resistance load without loading the source. The body is a fourth terminal; if it is not tied to the source, V<sub>BS</sub> shifts V<sub>TN</sub>. Only a few universities teach body effect in depth, so this chapter ignores it.

figure.caption: Both curves are normalized to the same 40 dB middle-band level so only the corner is compared; the common-source stage begins falling near 100 kHz, while the source-follower stage holds its level until about 10 MHz.

spec.aria: Two gain curves that are flat at 40 decibels and then fall; the common-source curve starts falling near 100 kilohertz, the source-follower curve near 10 megahertz.

examples.question: An NMOS CS amplifier has K<sub>n</sub> = 1 mA/V², V<sub>TN</sub> = 1 V, λ = 0.02 V⁻¹, I<sub>D</sub> = 1 mA, R<sub>D</sub> = 10 kΩ, and R<sub>L</sub> = 10 kΩ. (a) Find g<sub>m</sub> and r<sub>o</sub>. (b) Find the CS voltage gain. (c) Find the voltage gain for the same device as a source follower with R<sub>s</sub> = 1 kΩ.
steps: R<sub>D</sub> ∥ R<sub>L</sub> = (10 kΩ × 10 kΩ)/(10 kΩ + 10 kΩ) = 5 kΩ.
Source follower: g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>s</sub> = 2 mS × 1 kΩ = 2, so A<sub>v</sub> = 2/(1 + 2) = 0.667.
examples.answer: g<sub>m</sub> = 2 mS, r<sub>o</sub> = 50 kΩ, CS gain = −9.09, and source-follower gain = 0.667 (unitless).
examples.check:
K = 1e-3
I = 1e-3
lam = 0.02
RD = 10e3
RL = 10e3
gm = 2*(K*I)**0.5
ro = 1/(lam*I)
Rp = 1/(1/RD + 1/RL)
Rtot = 1/(1/Rp + 1/ro)
Av = -gm*Rtot
Rs = 1e3
Avsf = gm*Rs/(1 + gm*Rs)
print(f"{gm*1e3:.1f}")
print(f"{ro/1e3:.1f}")
print(f"{Av:.2f}")
print(f"{Avsf:.3f}")

traps: Using the BJT formula r<sub>e</sub> = 26 mV/I<sub>E</sub> for a FET. A FET has no r<sub>e</sub>; use g<sub>m</sub> = 2√(K<sub>n</sub>I<sub>D</sub>) and r<sub>o</sub> = 1/(λI<sub>D</sub>).
Leaving r<sub>o</sub> out when it is comparable to R<sub>D</sub> ∥ R<sub>L</sub>. The gain comes out too large.
Forgetting that an enhancement NMOS needs V<sub>GS</sub> above V<sub>TN</sub>. Below V<sub>TN</sub> the device is off and the model does not apply.
Dropping R<sub>L</sub>: CS sees R<sub>D</sub> ∥ R<sub>L</sub> ∥ r<sub>o</sub>, and a source follower uses R<sub>s</sub> ∥ R<sub>L</sub>.
Confusing signs: CS inverts; CG and CD do not. CD gain is also below one.

quiz.q: What does g<sub>m</sub> measure in the MOSFET small-signal model, and what is its unit?
quiz.a: The change in drain current for a small change in gate-source voltage at fixed drain-source voltage. Unit: A/V, also called the siemens (S).

quiz.q: Why is the input resistance of a CS stage much larger than that of a CE stage?
quiz.a: The CS input is the gate, which draws no steady current at low frequency, so bias resistors set the input resistance. A BJT base draws current, so its input resistance is finite, roughly r<sub>π</sub>.

quiz.q: An NMOS has K<sub>n</sub> = 0.5 mA/V² and I<sub>D</sub> = 0.5 mA. Find g<sub>m</sub>.
A CG stage uses a MOSFET with g<sub>m</sub> = 2 mS. Estimate its input resistance when r<sub>o</sub> is large.
A CS stage and a source follower use the same MOSFET at the same DC current. Explain why the CS stage can have voltage gain above one while the source follower has gain below one.
quiz.a: In CS, v<sub>gs</sub> equals the input voltage and the drain current change flows through R<sub>D</sub>, so the output can be g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>D</sub> times the input. In CD, the source moves with the input, so v<sub>gs</sub> = v<sub>in</sub> − v<sub>out</sub>. This negative feedback gives g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>s</sub>/(1 + g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>s</sub>), below one for finite R<sub>s</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does a CG stage not invert the signal?
quiz.a: The gate is at AC ground. If the source voltage rises, v<sub>gs</sub> falls, drain current falls, and drain voltage rises. Output follows input.

quiz.q: When must r<sub>o</sub> be included in the CS gain formula, and what happens if it is left out?
quiz.a: Include r<sub>o</sub> when it is comparable to R<sub>D</sub> ∥ R<sub>L</sub>, as in short-channel devices with large λ. Leaving it out makes predicted gain too large because the parallel output path is missed.

quiz.q: Write the formula for r<sub>o</sub> and define λ.
quiz.a: r<sub>o</sub> = 1/(λI<sub>D</sub>). λ is the channel-length modulation parameter in V⁻¹; it models how drain current changes slightly with drain-source voltage.

beyond: Not for the exam. IC designers often replace the source follower with a push-pull output stage because it wastes voltage headroom, but it survives inside op-amp outputs and low-dropout regulators. Radio-frequency designers use the CG stage as a low-noise input because its input impedance can be matched to 50 Ω. Body effect becomes a design variable in triple-well processes.
